Particular attention was given to frequency- and voltage-control hierarchies, hand-off between GFM and GFL modes, and the synchronization requirements associated with GFM operation in a weak-grid environment. This generic model provided the first end-to-end representation of coordinated GFM BESS + GFM wind + GFL wind + PV behavior at the full scale of the Wheatridge facility. Building on the EMT platform, the project developed the architecture for a real-time HIL testbed designed to evaluate inverter controls under realistic dynamic conditions. The HIL environment included real-time simulators, high-speed communication interfaces, and firmware-in-the-loop integration for inverter control systems. Initial HIL tests verified timing fidelity, synchronization performance, and controller stability during voltage dips, frequency events, and reference changes. These tests demonstrated that the control firmware could operate in real time against a dynamic EMT system without numerical instability, timing violations, or loss of control coherence. The HIL platform is technically capable of supporting system-level scenarios, such as phase-angle disturbances, weak-grid operation, and multi-resource interactions, that would be risky or impractical to evaluate directly in the field. This model captures the key GFM control behaviors, angle regulation, voltage-forming response, current-limiting behavior, and inertial active-power support in a format suitable for research, industry studies, and non-proprietary benchmarking. The project developed detailed EMT control representations for GFM Type-3 wind turbines, including both direct-voltage and virtual-admittance modes. These internal model structures were integrated into the generic EMT platform and used to assess multi-resource GFM/GFL interactions. The generic model reached an advanced developmental stage during BP1 and serves as the basis for a future public release once field-validation data become available. A major component of Task 3 was the system-level EMT study of the full hybrid plant. Using the generic EMT model, the team evaluated dynamic performance under voltage depressions, phase-angle disturbances, low short-circuit strength, and multi-resource interaction scenarios. These studies confirmed expected GFM characteristics, such as robust phase-angle regulation, damped frequency recovery, and improved voltage stiffness, while also identifying coordination requirements among inverter-level and plant-level controls. The EMT study results informed later tuning boundaries and served as a benchmark for future commissioning expectations. Concurrently, the team advanced development of a DC-coupled GFM system to support laboratory-based evaluation of PV+BESS configurations. This work included modeling of DC/DC converters, hybrid current-limiting behavior, and the dynamic coupling between AC-side disturbances and DC-side control functions.
